chunks: From him, from Safwan, from Mansur ibn Hazim, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man wishes to designate a specific person to purchase goods on his behalf (as a loan/advance), so that person says to him, 'I am more knowledgeable about my needs than you, so give me the money so I may buy it.' He takes the dirhams, buys his need, then brings it to the man who owns the money and delivers it to him. The Imam said: 'Is it not that if he wishes, he buys, and if he wishes, he leaves it, and if the seller wishes, he sells it, and if he wishes, he does not sell?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'There is no objection (it is valid).'

key_terms.أَبْصَرُ بِحَاجَتِي: More knowledgeable about my needs (referring to the buyer's discretion).
key_terms.عِينَةً: A specific type of loan or advance purchase where goods are bought on behalf of the lender.
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: There is no objection / It is permissible (a common legal ruling phrase).

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to give someone money to buy goods for you as a form of loan or advance payment?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) validates the practice of entrusting funds for specific purchases, clarifying that the transaction remains valid because both the buyer and seller retain independent discretion (*ikhtiyar*) to accept or reject the deal. This ruling underscores the flexibility of commercial contracts in Shia jurisprudence, distinguishing it from rigid obligations and ensuring that the core elements of consent are preserved in such agency-based transactions.
